records.content:
This Project Pythia Cookbook covers supervised machine learning readiness on a climate-model large ensemble: one classification
question — does the autumn ENSO state predict a wet Front Range winter? — answered on NSF NCAR’s own


CESM2 Large Ensemble (the AWS Open Data copy; no account needed),
walked along the analysis spine of NSF Unidata’s


Supervised Machine Learning Readiness, in seven short chapters.

This cookbook is for Earth system scientists, engineers and software staff who know Python (at the level of the


Xarray tutorial) and want to evaluate a machine-learning model honestly. Chapters 1–4 are the path for
someone new to machine learning; chapters 5–7 add the evaluation depth: paired tests, a held-out test, and an out-of-period test. The seven chapters
take about 1 hour 45 minutes, and each runs on its own in under a minute from a committed table.

records.content:
The closest neighbour, in the ProjectPythia organisation though not yet listed in the gallery, is the 

Precipitation Machine Learning Cookbook, a short
scikit-learn introduction (a regression of dew point on temperature, pressure and wind) that accompanies Unidata’s CyberTraining. The


CESM LENS on AWS Cookbook covers reading the CESM1 Large Ensemble, and the


scikit-learn Argo (also not yet listed), 

Landsat ML,


xbatcher ML and 

EO Data Science
cookbooks apply machine learning to other data. None yet walks a newcomer through a supervised classifier on a large ensemble,
where the members themselves are the unit the split has to respect.

So this cookbook changes one of Unidata’s steps on purpose, and adds to two others: the split is by ensemble member, and the forced response and the
wet threshold are fit on training members only. Chapter 3 measures what a member-blind split or a transform fitted before the split
would do to the score, rather than assuming it. Refinements are promoted on a paired test with a corrected standard error, and the result
is always read against the base rate of the same winters.

By the end you will be able to:

explain the steps of a supervised analysis (framing → data → split → train → validate → refine → test → justify) and name the failure each step guards against;

build and validate a classification model on a climate-model ensemble, reporting precision, recall and a confusion matrix;

compare refinement trials as a paired test across runs, so a gap inside the run-to-run spread is not read as a difference;

justify the chosen model honestly on measured performance and cost, including when nothing beats the base rate.

The signal is weak. The straight-line relation between autumn Niño 3.4 and winter precipitation is indistinguishable from zero. The final model,
gradient boosting at the base-rate threshold, shows a small precision edge on the held-out members, but that test is not blind: the same 20 members were scored during development, with four models, and the final model was registered after those
scores had been seen. Chapter 7 tests the edge on those members’ untouched SSP3-7.0 winters (2016–2100), under
a protocol written before that data was read (self-attested; it ships as notebooks/data/ssp370-test-protocol.md). The edge is not
confirmed: it does not replicate under the rule fixed before the run, but the test was small. A true edge of chapter 6’s size would
have cleared it only about 42% of the time (chapter 7 prints this), so the result neither confirms nor rules out an edge of that size in CESM2’s
SSP3-7.0 winters (the interval holds both 0 and chapter 6’s +0.018). Chapter 6 states the limits: a
model-world study, on a ~1° grid, of total precipitation, in DJF, for a box that crosses the Divide.

and split and goes on to a small neural network; nothing in it is needed here.

The person who acts on the answer is a forecaster drafting a local winter-outlook briefing, such as NWS Boulder’s (2020) or NWS
Pueblo’s (2025). The SON mean is complete only on 30 November, so this input serves a December update at zero lead; those two briefings were issued, by their contents, around September and October, before it exists, and would need an earlier input (JAS or ASO: a parameter edit and a
rebuild). Pueblo’s relays the Climate Prediction Center’s official lean and reports what the ENSO state statistically
suggests locally. A “wet” call right more often than the base rate, without missing most wet winters, would be the precondition for testing
that on observed winters (every score here is CESM2 against CESM2), beside CPC’s “equal chances”, as Pueblo’s 2025 briefing did: “Statistically, warmer and drier SE CO, but CPC’s forecast is equal chances …”.

Every parameter in lensml.py is a design decision with its reason; changing one is a trial you record. The seed is declared once and
passed down, never np.random.seed() (scikit-learn’s Common pitfalls, §12.3.3). The figure draws the two boxes from those
parameters.

def span(box):
    """A box as degrees with hemispheres, from its slices on the 0-360 grid."""
    y0, y1 = box["lat"].start, box["lat"].stop
    x0, x1 = box["lon"].start, box["lon"].stop

    def lat(y):
        return f"{abs(y):g}°{'S' if y < 0 else 'N'}"

    def lon(x):
        return f"{x:g}°E" if x <= 180 else f"{360 - x:g}°W"

    return f"{lat(y0)}–{lat(y1)}, {lon(x0)}–{lon(x1)}"

Unidata opens every analysis with three questions, so that the target answers someone’s decision.

Try it: frame it yourself first

Before opening the worked answers, write your own: three simple solutions a model must beat, whether the requirements can be met, and
the question as one decision.

The worked answers

Does a simpler solution exist? Three, and a model is measured against them, not assumed to beat them.

Simple solution

What it predicts

What it sets

always-dry

“dry” every winter

a bar on accuracy only (wet precision and recall are 0)

always-wet

“wet” every winter

recall 1 at precision = the base rate: the bar every precision is read against

Niño-sign rule

“wet” when the autumn Niño 3.4 anomaly is positive

the physical prior (NWS Boulder east of the Divide: El Niño wetter, La Niña drier); no bar

Can machine learning requirements be met? On the data side, yes: the catalogue holds monthly PRECC, PRECL and TS for every
historical member in both forcing variants. On the physics side the honest prior is a small effect: Stagge et al. (2023) find the
ENSO winter-precipitation signal over the Intermountain West is a north–south dipole, “the northern pole … north of 40° N” and “the southern pole remains south of 35° N, with some northward creep along the eastern edge of the study area”. The
Front Range (about 38.5–40.5° N), in the eastern part of their area, sits mostly between them, its northern edge just past 40° N, and the northern pole’s sign reversed
(La Niña wetter). The signal is measured here, not assumed.

Which scientific question should be answered? Given the autumn Niño 3.4 state in a CESM2 LENS member, will that member’s coming
Front Range winter be wet — above the one pooled threshold that marks the upper third of the training members’ detrended winters?

The catalogue forces two design facts: there is no monthly PRECT, so the target is PRECC + PRECL; and there is no variable
named SST, so the Niño 3.4 index is built from atmospheric TS over open ocean. The first cell lists the six stores; the second
computes what a box subset reads. Offline, each prints OFFLINE and the chapter runs from the cache.

CATALOG_URL = "https://ncar-cesm2-lens.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/catalogs/aws-cesm2-le.json"
try:
    cat = intake.open_esm_datastore(CATALOG_URL)
    subset = cat.search(
        component="atm",
        frequency="monthly",
        experiment="historical",
        variable=["PRECC", "PRECL", "TS"],
    )
    print(
        f"catalogue last_updated: {cat.esmcat.last_updated}   "
        f"rows in catalogue: {len(cat.df)}   rows selected: {len(subset.df)}"
    )
    cols = [
        "variable",
        "forcing_variant",
        "units",
        "start_time",
        "end_time",
        "path",
    ]
    with pd.option_context(
        "display.max_colwidth", None
    ):  # the six paths in full
        display(subset.df[cols])
except Exception as err:  # no network, a DNS failure, S3 unreachable
    if os.environ.get("CI"):  # CI has network: a failure there is real
        raise
    cat = subset = None
    print(
        f"OFFLINE: the catalogue at {CATALOG_URL} could not be read "
        f"({type(err).__name__}). The Metadata Document's catalogue and store "
        "rows are *not printed this run*; every later cell runs from the cache."
    )





try:
    probe = xr.open_zarr(
        "s3://ncar-cesm2-lens/atm/monthly/cesm2LE-historical-cmip6-TS.zarr",
        consolidated=True,
        storage_options={"anon": True},
    )
except Exception as err:  # offline: the structure rows are not printed
    if os.environ.get("CI"):  # CI has network: a failure there is real
        raise
    probe = None
    print(
        f"OFFLINE: the TS store could not be opened ({type(err).__name__}); "
        "the dims, calendar and chunking rows are *not printed this run*."
    )
if probe is not None:
    print("dims      :", dict(probe.sizes))
    print("coords    :", list(probe.coords))
    print(
        "members   :",
        probe.member_id.values[:3],
        "…",
        "calendar:",
        type(probe.time.values[0]).__name__,
    )
    ch = tuple(int(c) for c in probe["TS"].encoding["chunks"])
    per_chunk = (
        int(np.prod(ch)) * probe["TS"].dtype.itemsize
    )  # bytes, uncompressed
    n_time_chunks = -(
        -probe.sizes["time"] // ch[1]
    )  # chunks along time per member
    per_member_var = n_time_chunks * per_chunk
    n_members = (
        2 * probe.member_id.size
    )  # two halves, each the size of this store
    print(
        f"chunking  : {ch} {probe['TS'].dtype} → {per_chunk / 1e6:.0f} MB per chunk "
        f"uncompressed; one member-variable ({probe.sizes['time']} months) = "
        f"{n_time_chunks} chunks × {per_chunk / 1e6:.0f} MB ≈ {per_member_var / 1e6:.0f} "
        f"MB read for any box subset; the derivation ({n_members} members × 3 "
        f"variables) ≈ {n_members * 3 * per_member_var / 1e9:.0f} GB"
    )

The raw SON Niño 3.4 box mean and the winter precipitation both carry a forced trend (the corr(…, year) lines below print it). A degree-FORCED_DEG polynomial in year, fit to the training-member ensemble mean, is
subtracted from every member, leaving its own departure: the ENSO state, not the decade. Otherwise the models would learn
time-of-century as ENSO skill.

Then the target: wet = 1 when detrended precipitation sits above the WET_QUANTILE of the pooled training members, one threshold
for every member. One curve is fit to both forcing halves together; the per-half base-rate check below supports pooling them, though it
cannot see every difference a forcing half could make (chapter 6, limit 6).

Why one threshold, fit on training members only

A per-member quantile would fix each member’s base rate by construction, and the per-half check below could never fail. Curve and
threshold are fit on training members and applied to everyone else, as a StandardScaler inside a Pipeline is (scikit-learn’s
Common pitfalls, §12.1–12.2), so every validation fold in chapters 3–5 refits them.

show(fit_transforms, apply_transforms)



TRANSFORMS = fit_transforms(table[is_train])  # fit on ALL training members
table = apply_transforms(table, TRANSFORMS)

records.content:
A forced path the curve missed survives as decades whose mean anomaly sits away from zero. The removal passes only if every
decade’s mean lies within ±DECADE_TOL standard errors; the forced-response removal line gives the verdict and the chance of a false alarm.

Why not test the correlation with year

The correlation of the anomaly with year is zero by construction for any FORCED_DEG >= 1, so it could never fail.

DECADE_TOL = 3.0
d = table[is_train]
decade = (d["winter"] // 10) * 10
for anom, raw in ANOMALIES.items():
    r = d[raw].corr(d["winter"])
    print(
        f"corr({raw:20s}, year) = {r:+.3f}   "
        "(the forced trend in the raw series, training members)"
    )
removal_ok, n_tests = True, 0
for anom in ANOMALIES:
    g = d.groupby(decade)[anom]
    z = g.mean() / (d[anom].std() / np.sqrt(g.size()))
    worst = z.abs().idxmax()
    ok = bool((z.abs() <= DECADE_TOL).all())
    removal_ok &= ok
    n_tests += len(z)
    print(
        f"{anom:12s} decade-mean anomaly in standard errors: worst {z[worst]:+.2f} "
        f"(the {worst}s) · tolerance ±{DECADE_TOL:.0f} → {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}"
    )
false_alarm = 1 - (1 - 2 * norm.sf(DECADE_TOL)) ** n_tests
verdict = (
    "PASS"
    if removal_ok
    else "FAIL — a forced path survived; change FORCED_DEG"
)
print(
    f"forced-response removal: {verdict}   ({n_tests} decade means; chance a "
    f"correct removal trips the tolerance somewhere ≈ {false_alarm:.0%})"
)

records.content:
scikit-learn’s guidance on grouped cross-validation: “all the samples in the validation fold come from groups that are not represented at
all in the paired training fold.” Three reasons make the member the group:

The question is about members never seen. A member-blind split scores new years of members the model already knows.

The transforms. Fit before the split, held-out winters would help fit the forced curve and wet threshold that label them — the
leak of a StandardScaler fit on the whole table. Both are refit inside each fold.

Dependence is measured, not assumed. After the fold check come the lag-1 table and a micro-sibling line that fails if members
sharing a start year move together; that line licenses not grouping siblings.

Micro-siblings, and why the check is run on this window

Rodgers et al. 2021 §2.2 warn of initial-condition memory after 1850 and analyse internal variability “after 1960”; they give no
figure for 1900, so this cookbook’s 1900 start rests on the check below, not on Rodgers. Micro-siblings are members sharing a start year: the project page’s micro-perturbation members — the i1231-style token in
member_id. The check correlates them against unrelated members over the window.

Beside chapter 2’s test members, the training members are split into N_FOLDS = min(N_FOLDS_MAX, training members) folds by
scikit-learn’s StratifiedGroupKFold: the groups keep each member whole, and stratifying balances wet winters across folds.

Which labels the stratification reads

The folds are stratified on the all-training labels, which decide only which members share a fold; the labels scored inside a fold are
refit on that fold’s training members.

N_FOLDS = S.n_folds


def grouped_folds(seed, n_folds):
    # member-grouped, class-balanced folds over the training members
    return StratifiedGroupKFold(
        n_splits=n_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=seed
    )


# the same folds as lensml.member_folds, which chapters 4-7 call
assert all(
    np.array_equal(a1, a2) and np.array_equal(b1, b2)
    for (a1, b1), (a2, b2) in zip(
        grouped_folds(RNG_SEED, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr),
        member_folds(RNG_SEED, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr),
        strict=True,
    )
)



print(
    f"base rate train {train.wet.mean():.3f}   (the test members' base rate is "
    "printed once, in chapter 6; nothing here reads their labels)"
)
print(
    f"N_FOLDS = min(N_FOLDS_MAX={N_FOLDS_MAX}, {S.n_train_members} training "
    f"members) = {N_FOLDS}"
)
for k, (a, b) in enumerate(
    grouped_folds(RNG_SEED, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr)
):
    assert not set(g_tr[a]) & set(g_tr[b]), f"fold {k} leaks members"
print(
    f"{N_FOLDS} member-grouped folds verified: no member appears in both the "
    "fitting and the scoring side of any fold"
)
if S.n_repeats_effective == 1:
    print(
        f"NOTE: leave-one-member-out; the trials use 1 fold draw, not {N_REPEATS}"
    )


def lag1(s):
    v = np.asarray(s, dtype=float)
    return float(np.corrcoef(v[:-1], v[1:])[0, 1])


dependence = (
    train.groupby("member_id")
    .agg(lag1_nino34_anom=("nino34_anom", lag1), lag1_wet=("wet", lag1))
    .round(3)
)
print(
    "\nlag-1 autocorrelation within training members (what consecutive winters "
    "of one member share):"
)
print(dependence.to_string())
print("mean:", dependence.mean().round(3).to_dict())

MICRO_STARTS = {"1231", "1251", "1281", "1301"}
start_year = {
    m: re.search(r"i(\d{4})p", m).group(1) for m in train.member_id.unique()
}
print(
    f"\ncorrelation between training members over {WINDOW[0]}–{WINDOW[1]} "
    "(micro-siblings share a start year; the memory check):"
)
for anom in ANOMALIES:
    wide = train.pivot(index="winter", columns="member_id", values=anom)
    corr = wide.corr()
    sib, unrel = [], []
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(wide.columns, 2):
        same = start_year[a] == start_year[b] and start_year[a] in MICRO_STARTS
        (sib if same else unrel).append(corr.loc[a, b])
    sib, unrel = np.array(sib), np.array(unrel)
    if len(sib) < 2 or len(unrel) < 2:
        print(f"{anom:12s} too few member pairs of one kind to compare")
        continue
    excess = sib.mean() - unrel.mean()
    se = np.sqrt(sib.var(ddof=1) / len(sib) + unrel.var(ddof=1) / len(unrel))
    if abs(excess) <= 2 * se:
        reading = (
            "PASS: no sibling excess detectable (|excess| ≤ 2 SE, SE a lower "
            "bound) — the member is taken as the unit"
        )
    else:
        reading = (
            "FAIL: siblings still move together — group the folds by start "
            "year, or start WINDOW later"
        )
    print(
        f"{anom:12s} micro-siblings {sib.mean():+.3f} ({len(sib)} pairs, SD "
        f"{sib.std(ddof=1):.3f}) · unrelated {unrel.mean():+.3f} ({len(unrel)} pairs, "
        f"SD {unrel.std(ddof=1):.3f}) · siblings − unrelated {excess:+.3f} (±{se:.3f}, "
        "a lower bound: the pairs share members, so they are not independent "
        f"draws) → {reading}"
    )

One loop scores every validation run in this cookbook. Per fold: refit the transforms on the fold’s training rows (unless
refit_transforms=False), .fit the model, .predict the held-out rows, and score them for the wet class.

def score_folds(model, rows, splits, refit_transforms=True):
    out = {m: [] for m in ['ap', 'precision', 'recall', 'accuracy']}
    cm = np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)  # rows = true, columns = predicted
    for a, b in splits:
        fit_rows, held_rows = rows.iloc[a], rows.iloc[b]
        if refit_transforms:  # curve and threshold from this fold only
            tf = fit_transforms(fit_rows)
            fit_rows = apply_transforms(fit_rows, tf)
            held_rows = apply_transforms(held_rows, tf)
        Xa, ya = fit_rows[FEATURES].values, fit_rows['wet'].values
        Xb, yb = held_rows[FEATURES].values, held_rows['wet'].values
        model.fit(Xa, ya)
        yhat = model.predict(Xb)
        p_wet = model.predict_proba(Xb)[:, 1]
        out['precision'].append(precision_score(yb, yhat, zero_division=0))
        out['recall'].append(recall_score(yb, yhat, zero_division=0))
        out['accuracy'].append(accuracy_score(yb, yhat))
        out['ap'].append(average_precision_score(yb, p_wet))
        cm += confusion_matrix(yb, yhat, labels=[0, 1])
    return {m: np.array(v) for m, v in out.items()}, cm

How to read the gaps, and what this cell costs chapter 5

A precision resting on a handful of calls makes any gap a non-test, so below one wet call per hundred winters the cell marks the gaps

CONTRAST_THRESHOLD = 1 - WET_QUANTILE  # the designed base rate
MIN_WET_CALL_SHARE = (
    0.01  # below this, precision and recall gaps are a NON-TEST
)


def contrast_model(seed):
    return FixedThresholdClassifier(
        GradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING_SETTINGS, random_state=seed),
        threshold=CONTRAST_THRESHOLD,
        response_method="predict_proba",
    )


arms = {
    "A member split, transforms refit in each fold   ": dict(
        runs=[], cm=np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    ),
    "B member split, transforms fit before the split ": dict(
        runs=[], cm=np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    ),
    "C member-blind split, transforms refit in fold  ": dict(
        runs=[], cm=np.zeros((2, 2), dtype=int)
    ),
}
_folds = list(grouped_folds(RNG_SEED, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr))
_s05, _cm05 = score_folds(
    GradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING_SETTINGS, random_state=RNG_SEED),
    train,
    _folds,
)
# the same scores as lensml.score_splits, which chapters 4-7 call
_s, _cm = score_folds(contrast_model(RNG_SEED), train, _folds)
_m, _mcm = score_splits(contrast_model(RNG_SEED), train, _folds)
assert all(np.allclose(_s[m], _m[m]) for m in _s)
assert np.array_equal(_cm, _mcm)
print(
    f"for reference — the same model at sklearn's default threshold 0.5 (arm A's "
    f"split, one fold draw): wet calls {int(_cm05[:, 1].sum())} of {int(_cm05.sum())} "
    f"scored winters ({_cm05[:, 1].sum() / _cm05.sum():.2%}), recall "
    f"{_s05['recall'].mean():.3f} — too few calls to read a gap in"
)
for rep in range(S.n_repeats_effective):
    seed = RNG_SEED + rep
    by_member = list(grouped_folds(seed, N_FOLDS).split(X_tr, y_tr, g_tr))
    shuffled = StratifiedKFold(
        n_splits=N_FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=seed
    )
    by_year = list(
        shuffled.split(X_tr, y_tr)
    )  # member-blind: winters shuffled
    plan = [(by_member, True), (by_member, False), (by_year, True)]
    for (label, store), (splits, refit) in zip(arms.items(), plan):
        s, cm = score_folds(
            contrast_model(seed), train, splits, refit_transforms=refit
        )
        store["runs"].append(s)
        store["cm"] += cm
METRICS = ["ap", "precision", "recall", "accuracy"]
pooled_arm = {
    label: {m: np.concatenate([s[m] for s in st["runs"]]) for m in METRICS}
    for label, st in arms.items()
}
ref = pooled_arm[next(iter(pooled_arm))]


def sd(v):
    return v.std(ddof=1) if len(v) > 1 else 0.0


print(
    f"boosting at threshold {CONTRAST_THRESHOLD:.3f} (the base rate; 0.5 is sklearn's "
    f"default), {S.n_repeats_effective} fold draw(s) × {N_FOLDS} folds per arm. Per arm: "
    "scores (mean ± per-fold SD) and wet calls; then gap = arm − A (mean ± SD of the "
    "per-fold gaps)"
)
for label, s in pooled_arm.items():
    cm = arms[label]["cm"]
    wet_calls, n_scored = int(cm[:, 1].sum()), int(cm.sum())
    share = wet_calls / n_scored
    print(
        f"{label} AP {s['ap'].mean():.3f}   precision {s['precision'].mean():.3f} ± "
        f"{sd(s['precision']):.3f}   recall {s['recall'].mean():.3f} ± "
        f"{sd(s['recall']):.3f}   accuracy {s['accuracy'].mean():.3f}   wet calls "
        f"{wet_calls} of {n_scored} scored winters ({share:.1%})"
    )
    gaps = {m: s[m] - ref[m] for m in ["ap", "precision", "recall"]}
    if share >= MIN_WET_CALL_SHARE:
        reading = (
            f"gaps readable (wet calls ≥ {MIN_WET_CALL_SHARE:.0%} of winters)"
        )
    else:
        reading = "precision/recall gaps a NON-TEST: read AP only"
    print(
        f"{'':{len(label)}} gap vs A: AP {gaps['ap'].mean():+.4f} ± {sd(gaps['ap']):.4f}"
        f"   precision {gaps['precision'].mean():+.4f} ± {sd(gaps['precision']):.4f}   "
        f"recall {gaps['recall'].mean():+.4f} ± {sd(gaps['recall']):.4f}   → {reading}"
    )

Read each arm’s gap vs A line against the ± beside it: the leaks barely bite. The mean: line under the lag-1 table gives
lag1_wet near zero, so arm C has little to learn from a member’s other years. A small gap measures this design; it is not a licence.

Why the gaps are small, and when they would not be

No within-member persistence to memorise. With lag1_wet near zero, one wet winter says almost nothing about the next in the
same member. The input’s lag-1 is negative, not positive — no run of similar autumns either.

The input carries no member identity. With one detrended Niño 3.4 value per winter, nothing in a row tells the model which member
it came from, so it cannot memorise a member even when it has seen one.

The transforms are smooth fits to many members. A cubic in year through the mean of many training members, and one pooled
quantile, barely move when one fold’s members are left out — so fitting them before the split (arm B) leaks almost nothing.

With a member-specific input (a member’s own past winters, say) or transforms fit on fewer members, the same cell is where a member
split earns its keep.

Always-dry bars accuracy, always-wet bars precision (at the base rate), and the sign rule is the prior every rung must beat.

Why these three rungs

Rung 1 because one log-odds coefficient is the first thing a scientist wants to read. Rung 2 because it can bend where a line cannot — does the signal live only in strong events, as NWS Boulder’s “moderate to strong”
suggests? — under a depth cap. Rung 3 as the most flexible model
a one-input table can justify; the table is small, so the guide’s own note points at GradientBoostingClassifier rather than the
histogram variant. The costs: rung 1 assumes a linear boundary; a tree “can be unstable” and overfits without a depth or leaf limit;
boosting, “an excellent model … for tabular data”, costs run time, readability and more settings to record.

Seeds and Pipelines

Every estimator with randomness takes random_state=seed from the declared RNG_SEED, so a fit can be rerun, and scaling sits inside a Pipeline,
so a transform never sees the scoring side of a fold.

The cell builds all six; SignRule, the one custom estimator, prints its source. The asserts check the six against lensml.ladder,
which chapters 5–7 reuse.

The decision is a statistical statement in a briefing, and the two errors cost differently. A missed wet winter (recall falls) leaves the briefing at
CPC’s “equal chances” — a cheap miss. A false alarm (precision falls) puts “statistically wetter” in a briefing before a dry winter —
the costlier error, this cookbook assumes, for an office whose briefing is read as guidance.

Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to the designed base rate (1 - WET_QUANTILE) trades precision for recall along the same ranking,
adding no skill: the threshold table below prints the same ap at both. The cell only shows this; a threshold you keep is a
chapter 5 trial (FixedThresholdClassifier), and once this table has been read, that trial is no longer blind.

# sklearn's default, and the designed base rate

records.content:
Unidata’s instruction is to run trials “until you are satisfied with the evaluation metrics, or they no longer improve with new
trials”. Each trial repeats the member-grouped folds
N_REPEATS times on the same draws for both models, so every fold gives one paired difference. The test is the Nadeau–Bengio
corrected paired t-test, written out below from scikit-learn’s example Statistical comparison of models using grid search
(BSD-3-Clause). It is one-sided: a candidate must beat the incumbent, so a loss prints p near 1.

Why the standard error is corrected

Fold scores come from overlapping training sets, so they are not independent and a plain paired t-test under-estimates the variance.
A plain test divides the variance of the k per-fold differences by k; corrected_std multiplies it by 1/k + n_test/n_train
instead. “Corrected” means the standard error, not multiplicity: it does nothing about running many tests. Two changes from the example: it took np.abs(t_stat) under a right-tailed label, so a loss would have printed a small p; and
a zero spread (identical scores in every fold) now returns t = 0, p = 1 instead of dividing by zero. The register prints _sd, the
plain per-fold SD of the differences, for scale; _t divides the gap by the corrected error, and _t is the test.

# Adapted from scikit-learn's example "Statistical comparison of models
# using grid search" (examples/model_selection/plot_grid_search_stats.py).
# Copyright (c) 2007-2026 The scikit-learn developers. BSD-3-Clause; full
# text in LICENSES/scikit-learn-BSD-3-Clause.txt.


def corrected_std(differences, n_train, n_test):
    """Corrects standard deviation using Nadeau and Bengio's approach."""
    kr = len(differences)
    corrected_var = np.var(differences, ddof=1) * (1 / kr + n_test / n_train)
    return np.sqrt(corrected_var)


def compute_corrected_ttest(differences, df, n_train, n_test):
    """Computes right-tailed paired t-test with corrected variance."""
    mean = np.mean(differences)
    std = corrected_std(differences, n_train, n_test)
    if std == 0:  # added: identical scores in every fold (guards 0/0)
        return 0.0, 1.0
    t_stat = mean / std
    # changed from the example: t_stat, not np.abs(t_stat), so the test is
    # right-tailed as the docstring says and a LOSS prints p near 1
    p_val = t_dist.sf(t_stat, df)
    return t_stat, p_val

records.content:
Recall alone rewards calling wet always; precision alone, almost never. So a candidate is promoted only if one of the two improves
measurably — p < 0.05 with a positive gap — while the other does not fall on average (mean gap ≥ 0). Each register row carries
both tests and the wet-call share (called_wet_cand, called_wet_inc).

The example warns that “[I]f multiple models are statistically compared, a multiple comparisons correction is needed when using the
frequentist approach”. Each p here is uncorrected, so the register bounds the looks at MAX_TESTED_TRIALS rows, two metrics each,
and prints the Bonferroni line (0.05 ÷ the looks so far). A p between that line and 0.05 is a promotion under the uncorrected
rule only. The line counts only this register’s looks.

What the rule cannot see

It compares a candidate with the incumbent only, and the first incumbent is the sign rule. If the sign rule’s precision sits below
the always-wet bar (chapter 4), a candidate with no skill at all — precision merely at the base rate — can beat it. Read such a
promotion as a promotion over the sign rule, not as skill; chapter 6 reads the tested model against the base rate of the same winters.

records.content:
The cell below redoes the test as arithmetic on one register pair (by default the last promotion, on its metric): per-fold differences,
corrected standard error, t, and the one-sided p from scipy. A loss prints p near 1, so it also reads the left tail. Change
PAIR_A, PAIR_B or HAND_METRIC, and say whether the lead is a measured difference.

last = promoted[-1] if promoted else reg.rows[-1]
PAIR_A, PAIR_B = (
    last["incumbent"],
    last["candidate"],
)  # any two names in the register
promoted_on = (
    last["verdict"].split(":")[1].split()[0]
    if last["verdict"].startswith("promoted")
    else None
)
HAND_METRIC = promoted_on or "precision"
print(
    f"default pair: register row {last['trial']} ({last['candidate']} vs "
    f"{last['incumbent']}, verdict '{last['verdict']}') → metric {HAND_METRIC}"
    + ("" if promoted_on else "  (nothing promoted: precision by default)")
)

n_test = len(train) // S.n_folds
n_train = len(train) - n_test  # exactly as compare() sets them
a, b = reg.scores[PAIR_A][HAND_METRIC], reg.scores[PAIR_B][HAND_METRIC]
diff = b - a  # one paired difference per fold: candidate minus incumbent
k = len(diff)
df_hand = k - 1
sd_hand = diff.std(ddof=1)  # the plain per-fold SD
se_hand = np.sqrt(sd_hand**2 * (1 / k + n_test / n_train))  # corrected SE
if se_hand == 0:  # identical scores in every fold
    t_hand, p_hand = 0.0, 1.0
else:
    t_hand = diff.mean() / se_hand
    p_hand = t_dist.sf(t_hand, df_hand)  # one-sided: the RIGHT tail
p_loss = t_dist.cdf(t_hand, df_hand)  # the LEFT tail: small when PAIR_B lost

# the hand arithmetic == the functions above == lensml's, on this pair
assert np.isclose(se_hand, corrected_std(diff, n_train, n_test))
ref = lensml.compare(
    reg.scores[PAIR_A], reg.scores[PAIR_B], len(train), S.n_folds, HAND_METRIC
)
assert np.allclose(
    [t_hand, p_hand],
    compute_corrected_ttest(diff, df_hand, n_train, n_test),
)
assert np.allclose(
    [t_hand, p_hand], [ref[f"{HAND_METRIC}_t"], ref[f"{HAND_METRIC}_p"]]
)
for r in reg.rows:  # ... and on every register row, so the two cannot drift
    inc, cand = reg.scores[r["incumbent"]], reg.scores[r["candidate"]]
    for m in ("recall", "precision"):
        d = cand[m] - inc[m]
        ref = lensml.compare(inc, cand, len(train), S.n_folds, m)
        assert np.allclose(
            compute_corrected_ttest(d, len(d) - 1, n_train, n_test),
            [ref[f"{m}_t"], ref[f"{m}_p"]],
        )

print(
    f"{PAIR_B} − {PAIR_A} on {HAND_METRIC}: {len(diff)} paired fold scores   "
    f"n_train = {n_train}   n_test = {n_test}"
)
print(
    f"means {b.mean():.3f} vs {a.mean():.3f}   gap {diff.mean():+.4f}   per-fold SD of "
    f"the gap {sd_hand:.4f}   corrected standard error "
    f"{se_hand:.4f}  (the spread the test uses)"
)
if p_hand < 0.05:
    reading = (
        f"p < 0.05: a measured GAIN for {PAIR_B} under the uncorrected rule; "
        "read it against the Bonferroni line below"
    )
elif p_loss < 0.05:
    reading = (
        f"a measured LOSS for {PAIR_B}: {abs(t_hand):.1f} corrected standard errors "
        f"(left-tail p = {show_p(p_loss)})"
    )
else:
    reading = "NOT a measured difference (neither tail under 0.05)"
print(f"t = {t_hand:.2f}   p = {show_p(p_hand)}   →  {reading}")
reg.bonferroni_line()

        m: np.flatnonzero(test["member_id"].values == m)
        for m in test["member_id"].unique()
    }
    names = list(member_rows)
    point = {
        "precision − base rate": precision_score(

        )
        - y_te.mean(),
        "AP − base rate": average_precision_score(y_te, score_te)
        - y_te.mean(),
    }
    draws = {k: [] for k in point}
    for _ in range(N_BOOT):
        picked = boot_rng.choice(names, size=len(names), replace=True)
        pick = np.concatenate([member_rows[m] for m in picked])
        yb, hb, sb = y_te[pick], yhat_te[pick], score_te[pick]

            precision_score(yb, hb, zero_division=0) - yb.mean()
        )
        draws["AP − base rate"].append(

Unidata’s closing instruction: “No matter your final decision, the most important aspect is your ability to justify it using data and a
robust evaluation.”

The costlier error (chapter 4’s assumption) is a false alarm: “statistically wetter” in a briefing before a dry winter. Per the break-even line,
saying “wetter” pays only if a false alarm costs less than the printed fraction of a hit; the always-wet's break-even line gives the
same for calling every winter wet, and the gap is all the model adds. In this model world, an office that weighs a false
alarm as heavily as a hit would gain nothing over CPC’s “equal chances”. The precision edge (the interval line) is small and
provisional, and chapter 7’s test does not replicate it.

Why precision alone sets the false alarms per hit

False alarms per hit = (1 − precision) / precision, so any model with precision below 0.5 makes more false alarms than hits, however
rarely it calls wet; the wet-call share only scales the two counts. The false alarms per hit line prints it.

The justification, in three labelled parts:

Does it deliver? The interval, false-alarm and break-even lines.

If not, say so plainly. The answer is the base rate; the briefing stays at “equal chances”.

The next change, and its cost. A new season or box: a parameter edit and a rebuild (chapter 1). A new input: a new box mean in
derive_member_winters and a rebuild (chapter 2). A snowfall target
(PRECSC + PRECSL): one more derivation.

A model world. CESM2 scored against CESM2, never observations: not the real Front Range.

CESM2’s own ENSO and teleconnection, biases included.

A ~1° grid, smoothing the orography Stagge et al. (2023) find amplifies the ENSO signal on western slopes.

The season. DJF; NWS Boulder stresses late winter and spring for El Niño and fall and spring for La Niña east of the
Divide, so DJF tests both halves only in part.

Total precipitation (PRECC + PRECL), not snowfall, and a wet-only target: the coldest decile is below the base rate in all three
samples (beyond 2 standard errors in two), a dry signal a classifier of wet winters cannot state as a “drier”
call; a dry-tercile target is the next change to try.

One forced-response curve for both forcing halves, so a half-specific forced path is absorbed, not tested. Rodgers et al. (2021, §2.3)
report that the halves’ different biomass-burning forcing has “a discernible impact on large-scale climate”, including “tropical
Pacific warming”, around 1990–2010; this cookbook does not test whether that shifts the Niño 3.4 input in those years.

A box that crosses the Divide: about half mountain, half plains. NWS Boulder states the La Niña-dry sign for “southwest and
eastern Colorado” in “moderate to strong La Niñas”, and the opposite for the “northwest and north central portions”, which the west column partly covers.

Not a blind test (the top of this chapter).

The limits in detail

Limit 3: Stagge et al. (2023) find the amplification on the Intermountain West’s western slopes. Limit 4: the NWS wording is
“particularly during the late winter and spring of moderate to strong El Niños”. Limit 6: the cmip6 and smbb halves share one curve and
one threshold; their per-half base rates agree in chapter 2. Limit 7: the box’s west column (centre 106.25°W, edges 106.875–105.625°W)
lies mostly on or west of the Continental Divide, and the middle column holds the foothills and the eastern high peaks (Pikes Peak, 105.04°W 38.84°N, is inside
it). Limit 8: the top of this chapter.

records.content:
The terms the chapters use, in the sense they use them.

Term

Meaning here

ENSO, Niño 3.4

El Niño–Southern Oscillation; the Niño 3.4 index is the anomaly of mean surface temperature over 5°S–5°N, 170°–120°W, the input here

SON, DJF

September–October–November (the autumn input) and December–January–February (the winter target)

forced response

the externally forced path every ensemble member shares by calendar year (warming, and its precipitation trend); removed so a model reads ENSO, not the decade

precision

of the winters a model calls wet, the share that were wet

recall

of the winters that were wet, the share the model called wet

AP (average precision)

precision at each threshold of the model’s ranking, weighted by the recall gained there; a ranking with no skill scores the base rate

base rate

the share of winters that are wet; a classifier with no skill has precision equal to it

wet-call share

the share of winters a classifier calls wet; a classifier with no skill has recall equal to it

ladder, rung

the candidate models in order of flexibility: rung 0 is three rules that fit nothing, rungs 1–3 are logistic regression, a decision tree and gradient boosting

trial

one recorded change, scored against the incumbent on the same folds

incumbent

the model currently ahead; a trial replaces it only if the promotion rule says so

register

the table of every trial, its paired-test results and its verdict

looks

the tests taken so far: two (recall, precision) per register row

Bonferroni line

0.05 divided by the looks; a p below 0.05 but above it is a promotion under the uncorrected rule only
